Part 1 sets out the case and the vocabulary: why social science is argued about at all, the matrix that separates reproducing from replicating, and the five analysts who reanalysed the claim that the day works on. The hands-on work comes at the end and runs into the first break, so that if your machine gives trouble you miss none of the talk. The part takes ninety minutes.

## 1. The plan of the day

**On the slides.** The facilitator sets out the plan of the day and its two kinds of aim, what you will understand and what you will be able to do, and the slides say what you do not need. Open the browser lab in a tab and leave it to load while the facilitator talks.

[Open the browser lab](../../cases/eu-frames/lab.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-primary target="_blank"}

## 2. The credibility of social science

**On the slides.** Follow the talk on what social science is for, on false positives and forking paths, and on incentives and questionable research practices. It ends on the red-card study, in which twenty-nine teams analysed one dataset, with the estimates of the teams grouped by the response distribution that each team assumed, a grouping to keep in mind for the rest of the day.

## 3. The three Rs

**On the slides.** The word 'replication' names three operations, which the slides set out as a matrix of data against analysis. The slides then turn to repeatability and credibility, a quick check on the matrix in peer review, and the practices of open research.

## 4. Multi100 from the inside

**On the slides.** The slides show what a Multi100 analyst received, the paper in brief, the two Multi100 tasks and how the results of the two tasks were put on a common scale. The slides end on a forest plot of the results of the five analysts, revealed one row at a time.

## 5. The browser lab and the workspace

**On the slides.** The slides compare the browser lab with the workspace and say what the tools cannot do.

## 6. Task 1 – The setup check

[Open the browser lab at Task 1](../../cases/eu-frames/lab.qmd#task-1-setup){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

In the browser lab, wait for the R engine, run the three setup cells, and confirm that the second reports 270 rows, 27 countries and 10 years. If you have installed the workspace, open its folder in your IDE instead and run `source("R/check_setup.R")` until it reports no failure. The aim is to reach the point at which a line of R runs and the panel is in front of you, and if you need more time, carry on into the break.

**By the end of the part** R runs on your machine, you can tell apart the three operations that go under the word 'replication', and you have the results of the five analysts in front of you as the puzzle that the rest of the day works on.
